title: Seeing but Not Believing: Probing the Disconnect Between Visual Attention and Answer Correctness in VLMs
claim: Attention shifts across depth from one modality to the other: early layers favor text, deeper layers favor the visual input.
layout: 1 panel, dual y-axes, layer index on x-axis, error bars
description: A single line plot with layer index (0 to 31) on the x-axis and two y-axes. The left axis, in blue, shows image relative attention per token (RAPT), from about 0.2 to 0.6. The right axis, in red, shows text RAPT, from about 10 to 30. The blue series uses circle markers and the red series uses square markers. Both have vertical error bars and faint dashed horizontal gridlines in matching colors. The red text curve starts low, climbs to a peak around layers 10 to 16, then drops sharply near layer 17. The blue image curve stays low and flat through the early layers, then rises to a peak around layers 19 to 24 before falling and fluctuating near the end. The two curves cross over mid-network, which is where the eye goes first. The colored, bolded axis labels tie each axis to its series.
caption: Relative attention per token (RAPT)$^1$ (y-axis) to text tokens (red) and image tokens (blue) across model layers (x-axis). While early layers strongly emphasize text, deeper layers progressively increase attention to images, showing a sequential transition from linguistic parsing to visual grounding within a single-token inference. Similar trends hold across different VLM families, please see Appendix [ref] for more results.
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) achieve strong results on multimodal tasks such as visual question answering, yet they can still fail even when the correct visual evidence is present. In this work, we systematically investigate whether these failures arise from not perceiving the evidence or from not leveraging it effectively. By examining layer-wise attention dynamics, we find that shallow layers focus primarily on text, while deeper layers sparsely but reliably attend to localized evidence regions. Surprisingly, VLMs often perceive the visual evidence when outputting incorrect answers, a phenomenon we term ``seeing but not believing'' that widely exists in major VLM families. Building on this, we introduce an inference-time intervention that highlights deep-layer evidence regions through selective attention-based masking. It requires no training and consistently improves accuracy across multiple families, including LLaVA, Qwen, Gemma, and InternVL. These results show that VLMs encode reliable evidence internally but under-utilize it, making such signals explicit can bridge the gap between perception and reasoning, advancing the diagnostic understanding and reliability of VLMs.
